subject: blood_bank
question: Carla expresses the blood group antigens Fya, Fyb, and Xga. James shows expressions of none of these antigens. What factor(s) may account for the absence of these antigens in James?
explanation:
The frequency of Duffy antigens Fya and Fyb varies with race. The Fy(a-b-) phenotype occurs in almost 70% of African Americans and is very rare in whites. Xga antigen is X-linked and, therefore, expressed more frequently in women (who may inherit the antigen from either parent) than in men.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.1; book question 3; continuous question 3. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Genetics/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: If anti-K reacts 3+ with a donor cell with a genotype KK and 2+ with a Kk cell, the antibody is demonstrating:
explanation:
Dosage is defined as an antibody reacting stronger with homozygous cells (e.g., KK) than with heterozygous cells (e.g., Kk). In addition to Kell, dosage effect is seen commonly with antigens M, N, S, s, Fya, Fyb, Jka, Jkb, and the antigens of the Rh system.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.1; book question 2; continuous question 2. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Genetics/Kell/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which genotype(s) will give rise to the Bombay phenotype?
explanation:
The Bombay phenotype will be expressed only when no H substance is present. The Oh type is expressed by the genotype hh. Bombay phenotypes produce naturally occurring anti-H, and their serum agglutinates group O red blood cells (RBCs) in addition to RBCs from persons who are groups A, B, and AB.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.1; book question 6; continuous question 6. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/ABO/Bombay/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: All of the following are routinely performed on a cord blood sample except:
explanation:
An antibody screen is not performed routinely on a cord blood sample because a baby does not make antibodies until about 6 months of age. Any antibodies detected in a cord blood sample come from the mother.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.9; book question 16; continuous question 189. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of laboratory operations/Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn/Cord blood/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: The alleged father of a child in a disputed case of paternity is blood group AB. The mother is group O, and the child is group O. What type of exclusion is this?
explanation:
An indirect/secondary/second order, exclusion occurs when a genetic marker is absent in the child but should have been transmitted by the alleged father. In this case, either A or B should be present in the child.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.1; book question 11; continuous question 11. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to verify test results/Genotype/Paternity testing/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: Acquired B antigens have been found in:
explanation:
The acquired B phenomenon is only seen in group A persons.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 4; continuous question 22. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental characteristics/ABO/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which of the following statements is true?
option_a: An individual with the BO genotype is homozygous for B antigen
option_b: An individual with the BB genotype is homozygous for B antigen
option_c: An individual with the OO genotype is heterozygous for O antigen
option_d: An individual with the AB phenotype is homozygous for A and B antigens
explanation:
An individual having the BB genotype has inherited the B gene from both parents and, therefore, is homozygous for B antigen.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.1; book question 4; continuous question 4. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Genetics/ABO/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which of the following distinguishes the A1 blood group from the A2 blood group?
option_a: A2 antigen will not react with anti-A, A1 will react strongly (4+)
option_b: An A2 person may form anti-A1; an A1 person will not form anti-A1
option_c: An A1 person may form anti-A2, an A2 person will not form anti-A1
option_d: A2 antigen will not react with anti-A from a nonimmunized donor; A1 will react with any anti-A
explanation:
The group A1 comprises both A1 and A antigens. Anti-A will react with both A1- and A2-positive RBCs. A person who is group A2 may form anti-A1, but an A1 person will not form anti-A1 (which would cause autoagglutination).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 1; continuous question 19. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/ABO blood group/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: An anti-M reacts strongly through all phases of testing. Which of the following techniques would not contribute to removing this reactivity so that more clinically significant antibodies may be revealed?
explanation:
Lowering the pH will actually enhance reactivity of anti-M. Prewarming (anti-M is a cold-reacting antibody), cold adsorption with homozygous M cells, and testing the serum with enzyme-treated RBCs (destroys M antigens) are all techniques to remove reactivity of anti-M.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.11; book question 9; continuous question 211. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody ID/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: Why do immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies, such as those formed against ABO antigens, have the ability to directly agglutinate RBCs and cause visible agglutination?
option_a: IgM antibodies are larger molecules and have the ability to bind more antigen
option_b: IgM antibodies tend to clump together more readily to bind more antigen
option_c: IgM antibodies are found in greater concentrations than IgG antibodies
option_d: IgM antibodies are not limited by subclass specificity
explanation:
An IgM molecule has the potential to bind up to 10 antigens compared with a molecule of IgG, which can bind only two.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.1; book question 15; continuous question 15. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Antibodies/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which blood group has the least amount of H antigen?
explanation:
The A1B blood group has the least amount of H antigen. This occurs because both A and B epitopes are present on RBCs, compromising the availability of H epitopes. A1B cells will yield weak reactions with anti-H lectin.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 8; continuous question 26. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological principles/ABO/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which of the following enhancement mediums decreases the zeta potential, allowing antibody and antigen to come closer together?
explanation:
LISS contains a reduced concentration of NaCl (0.2%) and results in a reduction in charged ions within the ionic cloud, decreasing the zeta potential and facilitating antigen–antibody interaction.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.1; book question 16; continuous question 16. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Antigens/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: A complete Rh typing for antigens C, c, D, E, and e revealed negative results for C, D, and E. How is the individual designated?
explanation:
Rh positive refers to the presence of D antigen; Rh negative refers to the absence of D antigen. These designations are for D antigen only and do not involve other Rh antigens.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 1; continuous question 37. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Rh typing/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: A physician orders 2 units of leukocyte-reduced RBCs. The patient is a 55-year-old male with anemia. He types as an AB negative, and his antibody screen is negative. There is only 1 unit of AB negative in inventory. What is the next blood type that should be given?
explanation:
Although giving Rh-positive RBCs to an Rh-negative patient would not harm the patient in this case, because he is male, giving A negative would be the first choice. You should not expose a patient to the D antigen, if possible, and the residual anti-B in a unit of A-negative packed cells is less immunogenic than giving B or O RBCs.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 19; continuous question 55. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate sources of errors/Rh systems/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: A 76-year-old female diagnosed with urosepsis was transfused with 2 units of packed RBCs. Her type was AB positive and she had a negative result on antibody screen. The units transfused were AB positive. Upon receiving the second unit, the patient became hypoxic with tachypnea. The clerical check result was acceptable, and the DAT was negative. She received 269 mL from the second unit before a reaction was called. Her temperature fell from 38°C to 36.4°C, her pulse increased from 72 to 90, and respirations rose from 35 to 41. Her BP was 110/70 mm Hg. The patient died approximately 12 hours after the reaction was called. What type of reaction was most likely present?
explanation:
This case emphasizes the statistic that not all causes of death are related to transfusion. The temperature dropped ruling out a febrile reaction; there was no evidence of pulmonary edema or hypotension seen with TRALI (and plasma products are more associated with TRALI compared with RBCs); and there was no sign of hives or itching, which are often associated with an allergic reaction.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 11; continuous question 121. Topic path: Blood bank/Correlate laboratory and clinical data/Transfusion reactions/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: A stem cell transplant recipient was retyped when she was transferred from another hospital. What is the most likely cause of the following results? Patient cells: Anti-A, neg Anti-B, 4+ Patient serum: A1 cells, neg B cells, neg
explanation:
The transplant recipient is probably taking immunosuppressive medication to increase graft survival. This can contribute to the loss of normal blood group antibodies as well as other types of antibodies.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 13; continuous question 31. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to recognize health and disease states/ABO discrepancy/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: What type RBCs can be transfused to an A2 person with anti-A1?
explanation:
A person who is in need of RBC transfusion and is an A2 with anti-A1 can be transfused with A or O cells because the anti-A1 is typically only reactive at room temperature.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 9; continuous question 27. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological principles/ABO/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: How is an individual with genotype Dce/dce classified?
explanation:
This individual has D antigen and is classified as Rh positive. Any genotype containing D antigen will be considered Rh positive.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 2; continuous question 38. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Rh typing/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What reaction would be the same for an A1 and an A2 person?
explanation:
Anti-A,B should react positively with group A or B and any subgroup of A or B (with exception of Am). An A1 (not A2) would react with anti-A1 lectin; only an A2 person with anti-A1 would give a positive reaction with A1 cells; an A2 would react more strongly with anti-H than A1.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 14; continuous question 32. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/ABO discrepancy/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What antibodies could an R1R1 make if exposed to R2R2 blood?
explanation:
The R1R1 (DCe/DCe) individual does not have the E or c antigen, and could make anti-E and anti-c antibodies when exposed to R2R2 cells (DcE/DcE).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 13; continuous question 49. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Rh antibodies/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: A 59-year-old male came to the emergency department of a community hospital complaining of dizziness and fatigue. History included no transfusions and a positive rheumatoid factor 1 year ago. His complete blood count (CBC) confirmed anemia. A sample was sent to the blood bank for typing and crossmatching. Upon receipt of the sample in the blood bank, the MLS noticed the ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) sample appeared very viscous. Fearing that the sample would clog the automated instrument, testing was performed by using the tube method. The initial results revealed the following: Anti-A Anti-B Anti-D Rh Control A1 cells B cells 0 0 4+ 2+ 4+ 4+ The patient’s RBCs were washed eight times with saline, and testing was repeated, giving the following results: Anti-A Anti-B Anti-D Rh Control A1 cells B cells 0 0 4+ 0 4+ 4+ The antibody screen was negative at the IS, 37°C, and AHG phases; the check cells were positive. Crossmatch testing using two O-positive donor units revealed 1+ at IS, and negative results at the 37°C and AHG phases. The check cells were positive. In light of the crossmatching results, what is the next course of action?
option_a: Use other donor cells for crossmatching
option_b: Perform a saline replacement for crossmatching
option_c: Run the crossmatching test using the Gel system
explanation:
The history of the patient correlates with abnormal plasma proteins causing a positive result with the Rh control. Perform a saline replacement technique to rectify the incompatible crossmatches at IS.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.11; book question 4; continuous question 206. Topic path: Blood bank/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Rh discrepancy/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: A patient tests positive for weak D but also appears to have anti-D in his serum. What may be the problem?
option_a: Mixup of samples or testing error
option_b: Most weak D individuals make anti-D
option_c: The problem could be caused by a disease state
option_d: A D mosaic may make antibodies to missing antigen parts
explanation:
The D antigen comprises different parts designated as a mosaic. If an individual lacks parts of the antigen, he or she may make antibodies to the missing parts if exposed to the whole D antigen.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 10; continuous question 46. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge to identify sources of error/Rh antibodies/2.

subject: blood_bank
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch4_immunohematology/panel_2.png]]
On Panel 2, which of the following antibodies could not be ruled out?
explanation:
To rule out an antibody, there should be a homozygous cell with the corresponding antigen that fails to react with serum. Of the choices, anti-C was not ruled out on Panel 2. To rule this antibody out, a cell that is homozygous for C and negative for K (the other probable antibody) would be run against patient serum. A positive reaction supports the presence of anti-C, whereas a negative reaction would rule out anti-C.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 23; continuous question 79. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody ID/3. Source panel attachment included.

subject: blood_bank
question: A 68-year-old female diagnosed with neutropenia and inflammation of the left hand was typed as A positive and received 1 packed RBC unit. The antibody screen was negative, and crossmatch was compatible. During the transfusion, her pulse was 94, and blood pressure (BP) rose from 114/59 mm Hg to 132/64 mm Hg. Temperature rose from 37.1°C before transfusion to 37.8°C 60 minutes after starting transfusion and then to 38.3°C upon completion. A post-transfusion specimen yielded plasma that was neither hemolyzed nor icteric, and a negative DAT. Post-transfusion urinalysis showed 1+ blood and protein with 10 RBCs/high-power field (hpf) microscopically. The clerical check result was acceptable. What type of reaction most likely occurred as a result of transfusion?
explanation:
The temperature rose from 37.1°C to 38.3°C. The DAT result was negative, and although blood was found on the urinalysis, microscopic RBCs were also found. Because intact RBCs are not caused by a transfusion reaction, the cause of hematuria was not likely transfusion related. A febrile nonhemolytic reaction is highly consistent with both symptoms and post-transfusion test results.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 9; continuous question 119. Topic path: Blood bank/Correlation of laboratory and clinical data/Transfusion reactions/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: What should be done if all forward and reverse ABO results are negative?
option_a: Perform additional testing, such as typing with anti-A1 lectin and anti-A,B
option_b: Incubate at 22°C or 4°C to enhance weak expression
option_c: Repeat the test with new reagents
explanation:
All negative results may be caused by weakened antigens or antibodies. Room temperature or lower incubation temperature may enhance expression of weakened antigens or antibodies.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 11; continuous question 29. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory and clinical data to specify additional tests/RBCs/ABO discrepancy/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which characteristics are true of all three of the following antibodies: anti-Fya, anti-Jka, and anti-K?
option_a: Detected at the IAT phase; may cause hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) and hemolytic transfusion reactions
option_c: Requires the IAT technique for detection; usually not associated with HDFN
option_d: Enhanced reactivity with enzyme-treated cells; may cause severe hemolytic transfusion reactions
explanation:
Anti-Fya, anti-Jka, and anti-K are usually detected at IAT and all may cause HDFN and transfusion reactions that may be hemolytic. Reactivity with anti-Fya is lost with enzyme-treated RBCs, but reactivity with anti-Jka is enhanced with enzyme-treated cells. Reactivity with anti-K is unaffected by enzyme-treated cells.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 15; continuous question 71. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody ID/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What does the 3+3 rule ascertain?
option_c: 95% confidence that the correct antibody has been identified
option_d: 95% confidence that the correct antibody has not been identified
explanation:
The 3+3 rule ascertains correct identification of antibody at a confidence level of 95%. For this level to be met, reagent RBCs are found containing target antigen to suspected antibody that react in test phase; likewise, reagent RBCs devoid of antigen will not react in test phase.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 12; continuous question 68. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Antibody ID/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: What should be done if a noticeable clot is found in an RBC unit?
option_a: Issue the unit; the blood will be filtered
option_b: Issue the unit; note the presence of a clot on the release form
option_c: Filter the unit in the blood bank before issue
explanation:
A unit having a noticeable clot should not be issued for transfusion to a patient. The clot may be an indication of contamination or bacterial growth.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 12; continuous question 135. Topic path: Blood bank/Select course of action/Hemotherapy/RBCs/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which antibody is frequently seen in patients with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA)?
explanation:
Anti-e is frequently implicated in cases of WAIHA. The corresponding antigen is characterized as high frequency in the Rh system and can mask the presence of other alloantibodies.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 8; continuous question 64. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Blood group antibodies/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: A patient’s antibody shows strong reactions in all test phases. All screen and panel cells are positive. Serum is then tested with a cord blood cell, and the reaction is negative. What antibody is suspected?
explanation:
Adult cells contain mostly I antigen, and anti-I would react with all adult cells found on screen or panel cells. Cord blood cells, however, contain mostly i antigen and would test negative or only weakly positive with anti-I.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 9; continuous question 65. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody ID/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: All of the following are reasons for performing an adsorption, except:
option_c: Confirmation of weak antigens on RBCs
option_d: Identification of antibodies causing a positive DAT
explanation:
Antibodies causing a positive DAT would be coating RBCs and would require elution, not adsorption, to identify them.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 22; continuous question 104. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody identification/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: All of the following are required tests on donor blood, except:
explanation:
Testing of donor blood for antibodies to CMV is not required. However, testing may be done on units intended for transfusion to low-birth-weight infants born to seronegative mothers or units used for intrauterine transfusion; units intended for immunocompromised patients who are seronegative; prospective transplant recipients who are seronegative; or transplant recipients who have received a seronegative organ. Leukocyte-reduced RBCs carry a reduced risk of transmitting CMV and are recommended for such patients when CMV testing has not been performed on donor units. The prevalence of anti-CMV in the population ranges from 40% to 90%.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.10; book question 9; continuous question 201. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Processing/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: If a patient has a positive DAT, should you perform a weak D test on the cells?
option_a: No, the cells are already coated with antibody
option_c: Yes, the immunoglobulin will not interfere with the test
option_d: Yes, Rh reagents are enhanced in protein media
explanation:
If a person has a positive DAT, the RBCs are coated with immunoglobulin. If a test for weak D were performed, the test would yield positive results independent of the presence or absence of D antigen on the RBCs.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 3; continuous question 39. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Rh typing/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: What sample is best for detecting complement-dependent antibodies?
option_a: Plasma stored at 4°C for no longer than 24 hours
option_b: Serum stored at 4°C for no longer than 48 hours
option_c: Either serum or plasma stored at 20°C to 24°C no longer than 6 hours
explanation:
Serum stored at 4°C for no longer than 48 hours preserves complement activity. Plasma is inappropriate because most anticoagulants chelate calcium needed for activation of complement. Heating the serum to 56°C destroys complement.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 19; continuous question 75. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Antibody ID/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which procedure would help to distinguish between anti-e and anti-Fya in an antibody mixture?
option_a: Lowering the pH of test serum
explanation:
Enzyme-treated cells will not react with Duffy antibodies. Rh antibodies react more strongly with enzyme-treated RBCs. An enzyme panel, therefore, would enhance reactivity of anti-e and destroy reactivity to anti-Fya.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 14; continuous question 70. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody ID/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: An antibody is detected in a pregnant woman and is suspected of being the cause of fetal distress. The antibody reacts at the IAT phase but does not react with DTT-treated cells. This antibody causes in vitro hemolysis. What is the most likely antibody specificity?
explanation:
Of the antibodies listed, only Lub is detected in the IAT phase, causes in vitro hemolysis, may cause HDFN, and does not react with DTT-treated cells.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 18; continuous question 74. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/Antibody ID/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: How much anticoagulant would have to be removed from the collection bag given a donor who weighs 90 lb?
explanation:
To determine the amount of anticoagulant to remove when the donor is less than 110 lb, divide weight by 110 lb, and multiply by 450 mL; divide that number by 100, and multiply by 14 (this gives the anticoagulant volume needed); then subtract this from 63 mL, which is the standard volume of anticoagulant in a 450 mL bag. The result is the amount of anticoagulant to remove.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 10; continuous question 163. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Donor collection/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: An antibody screen is reactive at the IAT phase of testing with all three cells of a three-cell screen, and the autocontrol is negative. What is a possible explanation for these results?
option_b: High-frequency alloantibody or a mixture of alloantibodies
explanation:
High-frequency alloantibodies or a mixture of alloantibodies may cause all three screening cells to be positive. A negative autocontrol would rule out autoantibodies.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 3; continuous question 85. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/Antibody ID/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: Can crossmatching be performed on October 14 using a patient sample drawn on October 12?
option_a: Yes, a new sample would not be needed
option_b: Yes, but only if the previous sample has no alloantibodies
option_c: No, a new sample is needed because the 2-day limit has expired
option_d: No, a new sample is needed for each testing
explanation:
Compatibility testing may be performed on a patient sample within 3 days of the scheduled transfusion; however, if the patient is pregnant or was transfused within 3 months, the sample must be less than 3 days old.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 5; continuous question 87. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Crossmatch/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What does a minor crossmatch consist of?
explanation:
A minor crossmatch consists of recipient RBCs and donor serum or plasma.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 4; continuous question 86. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of laboratory operations/Crossmatch/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which antibody would not be detected by group O screening cells?
explanation:
ABO antibodies are not detected by group O screening cells because O cells contain no A or B antigens.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 20; continuous question 76. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody ID/1.

subject: blood_bank
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch4_immunohematology/panel_2.png]]
Refer to Panel 2. Which antibody specificity is most likely present?
explanation:
The pattern fits anti-C at 37°C, which becomes stronger at the IAT phase. The additional antibody is anti-K, which appears only at the IAT phase.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.4; book question 22; continuous question 78. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Antibody ID/3. Source panel attachment included.

subject: blood_bank
question: Screening cells and major crossmatch are positive on IS only, and the autocontrol is negative. Identify the problem.
explanation:
A cold alloantibody would show a reaction with screening cells and donor units only at the IS phase. The negative autocontrol rules out autoantibodies and abnormal protein.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 13; continuous question 95. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/Incompatible crossmatch/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: SITUATION: An O-negative mother gave birth to a B-positive infant. The mother had no history of antibodies or transfusion. This was her first child. The baby was mildly jaundiced, and the DAT result was weakly positive with polyspecific antisera. What could have caused the positive DAT result?
option_a: Anti-D from the mother coating the infant RBCs
option_b: An alloantibody, such as anti-K, coating the infant RBCs
option_c: Maternal anti-B coating the infant RBCs
option_d: Maternal anti-A, B coating the infant RBCs
explanation:
Anti-A,B is an IgG antibody and can cross the placenta and attach to infant cells. It is known as a single entity as opposed to separate antibodies. Anti-D would not be the cause because this is the first pregnancy. Anti-K is not the cause because there is no history of alloantibodies or past transfusions.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.9; book question 18; continuous question 191. Topic path: Blood bank/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: What ABO types may donate to any other ABO type?
option_a: A negative, B negative, AB negative, O negative
option_d: AB negative, A negative, B negative
explanation:
An O-negative individual has no A or B antigens and may donate RBCs to any other ABO type.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 7; continuous question 89. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Crossmatch/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: A type and screen was performed on a 32-year-old woman, and the patient was typed as AB negative. There are no AB-negative units in the blood bank. What should be done?
option_a: Order AB-negative units from a blood supplier
option_b: Check inventory of A-, B-, and O-negative units
option_c: Ask the patient to make a preoperative autologous donation
option_d: Nothing—the blood will probably not be used
explanation:
An AB person is the universal recipient and may receive any blood type; because only a type and screen were ordered and blood may not be used, check inventory for A-, B-, and O-negative units.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 6; continuous question 88. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Crossmatch/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which of the following is not a requirement for electronic crossmatching?
option_a: The computer system contains logic to prevent assignment and release of ABO-incompatible blood
option_b: There are concordant results of at least two determinations of the recipient’s ABO type on record, one of which is from the current sample
option_c: Critical elements of the system have been validated on site
option_d: There are concordant results of at least one determination of the recipient’s ABO type on file
explanation:
ABO determinations must be concordant on at least two occasions, including the current sample.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 11; continuous question 93. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Crossmatch/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Six units are crossmatched. Five units are compatible, one unit is incompatible, and the recipient’s antibody screen is negative. Identify the problem:
option_a: Patient may have an alloantibody to a high-frequency antigen
option_b: Patient may have an abnormal protein
option_c: Donor unit may have a positive DAT
option_d: Donor may have a high-frequency antigen
explanation:
The incompatible donor unit may have an antibody coating the RBCs, or the patient may have an alloantibody to a low-frequency antigen. An alloantibody to a high- frequency antigen would agglutinate all units and screening cells.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 14; continuous question 96. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/Incompatible crossmatch/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which offspring is not possible from a mother who is R1R2 and a father who is R1r?
explanation:
DcE/DcE (R2R2) is not possible because R2 can be inherited only from the mother and is not present in the father.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 11; continuous question 47. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to verify test results/Rh system/Paternity testing/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: How long must a recipient sample be kept in the blood bank after compatibility testing?
explanation:
According to the American Association of Blood Banks (AABB) standards, the recipient sample must be kept for 7 days after compatibility testing.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 23; continuous question 105. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Compatibility/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: A patient is typed as AB positive. Two units of blood have been ordered by the physician. Currently, the inventory shows no AB units, 10 A-positive units, 1 A-negative unit, 5 B-positive units, and 20 O-positive units. Which should be set up for the major crossmatch?
option_d: Call another blood supplier for type-specific blood
explanation:
The type chosen should be A-positive RBC units. Although all choices would be compatible, the first choice should be A-positive because this unit will contain residual plasma anti-B. Anti-B is less immunogenic than anti-A, which would be present, albeit in small amounts, in B-positive and O-positive units.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 26; continuous question 108. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Compatibility/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What are the compatibility requirements for an autologous unit?
explanation:
The only requirement for transfusing an autologous unit is a check of the ABO and Rh types.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 25; continuous question 107. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Compatibility/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: All of the following are interventions for fetal distress caused by maternal antibodies attacking fetal cells except:
option_c: Transfusion of antigen-positive cells to the mother
option_d: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV)
explanation:
Transfusion of antigen-positive cells to the mother who already has an antibody might cause a transfusion reaction and/or evoke an even stronger antibody response, possibly causing more harm to the fetus.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.9; book question 4; continuous question 177. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn/Clinical interventions/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What is the pathophysiological cause surrounding anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions?
option_a: Antibody in patient’s serum is detected 3 to 7 days after transfusion and is attached to donor RBCs
option_b: Donor plasma has reagins (IgE or IgA) that combine with allergens in patient’s plasma
option_c: Patient is deficient in IgE and develops IgE antibodies via sensitization as a result of transfusion or pregnancy
option_d: Patient is deficient in IgA and develops IgA antibodies via sensitization as a result of transfusion or pregnancy
explanation:
Anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions are the most severe form of allergic transfusion reaction and are associated with deficient or absent IgA in the patients, allowing the formation of anti-IgA. These patients must be transfused with washed cellular products where the plasma has been removed.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 2; continuous question 112. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological principles/Transfusion reactions/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: What would be the result of group A blood given to a group O patient?
explanation:
Group A blood given to a group O patient would cause an immediate hemolytic transfusion reaction because a group O patient has anti-A and anti-B antibodies and would destroy A cells.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 6; continuous question 116. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Transfusion reactions/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: When may IS crossmatching be performed?
option_a: When a patient is being massively transfused
option_b: When there is no history of antibodies and the current antibody screen is negative
option_c: When blood is being emergency released
option_d: When a patient has not been transfused in the past 3 months
explanation:
IS crossmatching may be performed when the patient has no history of antibodies and the current antibody screen is negative.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 28; continuous question 110. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of basic laboratory procedures/Crossmatch/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: All of the following are part of the preliminary evaluation of a transfusion reaction, except:
option_a: Check pre-and post-transfusion samples for color of serum
option_c: Perform DAT on the post-transfusion sample
option_d: Perform a panel on pre-and post-transfusion samples
explanation:
The preliminary evaluation of a transfusion reaction includes checking the color of serum and performing ABO and Rh checks and DAT on the post-transfusion sample. A panel would not be part of the preliminary workup.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 8; continuous question 118. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Transfusion reactions/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: A panel study has revealed the presence of patient alloantibodies. What is the first step in a major crossmatch?
option_a: Perform a DAT on patient cells and donor units
option_b: Antigen type patient cells and any donor cells to be crossmatched
option_c: Adsorb any antibodies from patient serum
option_d: Obtain a different enhancement medium for testing
explanation:
Antigen typing or phenotyping of the patient’s cells confirms the antibody identification; antigen typing of donor cells helps ensure the crossmatch of compatible donor units.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 17; continuous question 99. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply principles of special procedures/Incompatible crossmatch/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What may be found in the serum of a person who is exhibiting signs of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)?
explanation:
TRALI is associated with antibodies to human leukocyte antigens or neutrophil antigens, which react with the patient’s granulocytes and cause acute respiratory insufficiency.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 4; continuous question 114. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Transfusion reactions/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: A 52-year-old male received 2 units of packed RBCs as an outpatient in the intravenous (IV) therapy unit. He had had a head trauma 20 years ago and was quadriplegic. He had recurrent pneumonia and hematuria as a result of removal of a Foley catheter. His blood type was A positive, with previously identified anti-Fya. There was an ABO discrepancy, in that reverse typing with reagent A1 cells was positive. The MLS attributed this reaction to Fya antigen being present on the reagent A1 cells. The patient also had a cold autoantibody. Two units of A-positive packed cells were crossmatched that were Fya negative and were compatible. One unit was transfused at 11:30 a.m. without incident. The second unit was transfused at 2:16 p.m. and stopped at 3:55 p.m. because of reddish brown–tinged urine found in his collection bag. A post-transfusion specimen yielded a positive DAT and plasma that was grossly hemolyzed. A prewarm crossmatch was incompatible in both the pre-and post-transfusion specimens. Anti-E and anti-c were present in the post-transfusion specimen. What reaction was most likely present?
explanation:
This case represents an acute hemolytic reaction where the patient had previous sensitization to E and c antigens. Given the history of anti-Fya, an assumption was made that anti-Fya was the cause of the positive reverse type with A1 cells, even though this antibody does not react at the IS phase. This brings to light the importance of running a panel whenever the patient has a positive antibody screen, regardless of previous results. Hemoglobinuria, a positive DAT, and the hemolyzed post-transfusion specimen all are consistent with an acute hemolytic reaction.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 12; continuous question 122. Topic path: Blood bank/Correlate laboratory and clinical data/Transfusion reactions/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: A 92-year-old male diagnosed with anemia and episodes of frequent falling was typed as B negative and transfused with 1 unit of packed RBCs, also B negative. He had not been recently transfused, and the antibody screen was negative. During the transfusion, his temperature rose from 36.2°C to 36.4°C, his pulse from 96 to 124, respirations from 18 to 20, and BP from 127/81 mm Hg to 174/83 mm Hg. He was transfused with 205 mL before a reaction was called by the transfusionist. The post-transfusion specimen DAT result was negative, and the clerical check result was acceptable. Urinalysis showed 1+ blood with 5 RBCs microscopically. Other symptoms included tachycardia and flushing. What reaction had most likely taken place?
explanation:
The tachycardia, increased pulse, and volume transfused before a reaction was called are consistent with volume overload. The temperature change did not meet criteria for a febrile reaction, and evidence for a hemolytic reaction is lacking.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 10; continuous question 120. Topic path: Blood bank/Correlation of laboratory and clinical data/Transfusion reaction/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: What does the genotype —/— represent in the Rh system?
explanation:
A person who is Rhnull shows no Rh antigens on his or her RBCs. Loss of Rh antigens is very unlikely to happen because Rh antigens are integral parts of the RBC membrane. The Rhnull phenotype can result from either genetic suppression of the Rh genes or inheritance of amorphic genes at the Rh locus.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 14; continuous question 50. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/Rh system/Rh antigens/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What antibodies are formed by a Bombay phenotype individual?
explanation:
A Bombay phenotype individual does not express A, B, or H antigens; therefore, anti- A, -B, and -H are formed. Because a Bombay phenotype individual has three antibodies, the only compatible blood must be from another Bombay phenotype donor.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.2; book question 3; continuous question 21. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/ABO blood group/Bombay/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: What method can be employed to detect bacteria in random donor platelets?
explanation:
The FDA has mandated that pH and glucose can no longer be used as a screening test for platelets. The Verax PGD assay has been FDA approved for both single-donor platelets and random-donor platelets for bacteria screening.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 8; continuous question 131. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of laboratory operations/Blood components/Preparation of components/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: An 82-year-old male was admitted for renal failure. His type was B positive, and his antibody screen was negative. Two units of RBCs were ordered. The first unit was transfused at 1:00 p.m. without incident. The second was started at 4:15 p.m. and stopped at 5:12 p.m. after the nurse observed that the patient had died. Vital signs had been taken at 4:30 p.m. with no abnormalities. A transfusion reaction was called and the blood unit, tubing, and paperwork sent to the blood bank. There were no clinical manifestations noted on the paperwork, and no post-transfusion specimen was sent to the blood bank. What type of reaction most likely occurred?
explanation:
This example represents a situation where the pathologist was not provided with all information needed to interpret the reaction. There was no information on patient symptoms, the patient had received another unit of RBCs hours previously with no problems, and a postreaction specimen was not collected. Therefore, any serological abnormalities could not be identified. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommends collecting a postmortem specimen if a reaction is called so that the investigation of transfusion reaction can be completed. In this case, the pathologist interpreted the reaction as not related to transfusion because no symptoms were documented.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.6; book question 13; continuous question 123. Topic path: Blood bank/Correlate clinical and laboratory data/Transfusion reactions/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: A major crossmatch and screening cells are 2+ at the IS phase, 1+ at 37°C, and negative at the IAT phase. Identify the most likely problem.
explanation:
The reaction pattern fits that of a cold antibody reacting at the IS phase and of sufficient titer to persist at 37°C incubation. The reactions disappear in the IAT phase.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.5; book question 20; continuous question 102. Topic path: Blood bank/Evaluate laboratory data to make identifications/Incompatible crossmatch/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: A unit of packed RBCs is split using the open system. One of the half units is used. What may be done with the second half unit?
option_d: Must retain the original expiration date
explanation:
The other half unit must be issued within 24 hours, if an open system is used to split the unit.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 11; continuous question 134. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of laboratory operations/Blood components/RBCs/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What percentage of RBCs must be retained in leukocyte-reduced RBCs?
explanation:
An RBC unit that has been leukocyte reduced must retain 85% of original RBCs.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 20; continuous question 143. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Blood components/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Transfusion of an irradiated product is indicated in all of the following conditions except:
explanation:
WAIHA would not require irradiation unless the patient had an underlying immunosuppressive disorder.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 19; continuous question 142. Topic path: Blood bank/Select course of action/Hemotherapy/Irradiation/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: What is a special condition for the storage of platelets?
option_b: No other components may be stored with platelets
option_c: Platelets must be stored upright in separate containers
option_d: Platelets require constant agitation at 20°C to 24°C
explanation:
Platelets require constant agitation and are stored at temperatures between 20°C and 24°C. Cold-stored platelets (single donor [apheresis] platelets stored at 1-6°C for up to 3 days) may be used for actively bleeding patients, but are not approved for treating thrombocytopenia.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 18; continuous question 141. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Blood components/Processing/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Cryoprecipitate may be used to treat all of the following, except:
explanation:
Cryoprecipitate may be used to treat von Willebrand disease, hypofibrinogenemia, and factor XIII deficiency, but is not indicated in ITP. IVIG is the product of choice for ITP.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 13; continuous question 136. Topic path: Blood bank/Select best course of action/Hemotherapy/Cryo/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: What components(s) may be shipped together with FFP?
explanation:
FFP requires dry ice for shipment. Frozen RBCs and cryoprecipitate also require dry ice.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 23; continuous question 146. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Blood components/FFP/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: What component(s) is (are) indicated for patients who have anti-IgA antibodies?
explanation:
Patients with anti-IgA antibodies should not receive components containing plasma. Washed or deglycerolized RBCs can be issued.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 15; continuous question 138. Topic path: Blood bank/Select course of action/Hemotherapy/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: How does irradiation prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD)?
option_a: Gamma rays and x-rays destroy the lymphocytes’ ability to divide
option_b: X-rays cause lysis of the lymphocytes
option_d: Ultraviolet radiation induces apoptosis of lymphocytes
explanation:
Gamma rays or x-rays have the ability to prohibit a lymphocyte’s ability to divide, preventing TA-GVHD.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 25; continuous question 148. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Blood components/Stem cells/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which component has the longest expiration date?
explanation:
Frozen RBCs may be kept for up to 10 years, or longer if the transfusion service or blood center has a policy for extension beyond 10 years. FFP and cryoprecipitate stored at –18°C or lower expire in 1 year. If FFP is kept at –65°C or lower, the expiration time is 7 years. Platelet concentrates expire from 24 hours to 5 days, depending on the collection system used.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 26; continuous question 149. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Blood bank/Expiration date/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which of the following precludes acceptance of a plateletpheresis donor?
option_a: Platelet count of 75 × 109/L in a donor who is a frequent platelet donor
option_b: Plasma loss of 800 mL from plasmapheresis 1 week ago
explanation:
To be eligible for plateletpheresis, the platelet count should be greater than 150 × 109/L for a frequent platelet donor. Plasma loss exceeding 1,000 mL would be cause for rejection, but not 800 mL. A donor may donate 24 times a year, but not as frequent as once every 2 days in a 7-day period. A donor cannot ingest aspirin within 36 hours of platelet donation.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 5; continuous question 158. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Donor requirements/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: SITUATION: A 53-year-old woman donates blood at her place of employment. She weighs 150 lb and has a hemoglobin level of 13 g/dL. She is currently on warfarin and vitamin B12. Is she an acceptable donor?
option_d: No, her hemoglobin is too low
explanation:
Her age and hemoglobin meet donor criteria. However, because she is currently on warfarin, only RBCs can be prepared from her donation.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 2; continuous question 155. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Donor requirements/2.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which genotype usually shows the strongest reaction with anti-D?
explanation:
The phenotype that results from D–/D– is classified as enhanced D because it shows a stronger reaction than expected with anti-D. Such cells have a greater amount of D antigen than normal. This is thought to result from a larger quantity of precursors being available to the D genes because there is no competition from other Rh genes.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.3; book question 5; continuous question 41. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of fundamental biological characteristics/Rh typing/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: What is the number of WBCs permitted in a unit of leukocyte-reduced RBCs?
explanation:
RBCs that have been leukocyte reduced must have fewer than 5 × 106 WBCs per unit.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.7; book question 29; continuous question 152. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Blood components/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which physical examination result is cause for rejecting a whole blood donor?
explanation:
Diastolic pressure must not be higher than 100 mm Hg. Donors weighing less than 110 lb may donate up to 12% of their blood volume (volume = weight in kg/50 × 450 mL). Oral temperature must not be greater than 37.4°C (99.5°F). BP limits for donation are 180 mm Hg for systolic and 100 mm Hg for diastolic pressure. The limit for hemoglobin is 12.5 g/dL and for hematocrit 38%.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 7; continuous question 160. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Donor requirements/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which situation is not a cause for indefinite deferral of a donor?
option_a: Male donor whose father has been diagnosed with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)
option_b: Donation of a unit of blood that transmitted hepatitis B virus (HBV) to a recipient
option_c: Donor tested reactive for HBV by nucleic acid testing (NAT)
option_d: Accidental needlestick 1 year ago; negative for infectious disease
explanation:
An accidental needlestick would not be a cause for indefinite deferral of a donor. The deferral period is 1 year.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 8; continuous question 161. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Donor requirements/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: An autologous unit of whole blood was collected on a 33-year-old woman in preparation for a knee replacement procedure in 3 weeks. The whole blood unit had her hyphenated last name, first name, and last four digits of her social security number for identification. The laboratory computer system, however, only had her married name and first name, medical record number, and social security number. What should be done with this blood product?
option_b: Make the unit available for transfusion
option_c: Confirm the name with the donor, have admissions make the correction in the computer system, and then make the unit available for transfusion
option_d: Ensure that social security numbers match, confirm the name with the donor and have admissions make the correction in the computer system with the medical director’s approval, and then make the unit available for transfusion
explanation:
This is a common scenario with women who have recently married, and have not changed their license or other form of identification given to the collection facility. Checking that other demographic information matches is sufficient, if approved by the medical director, because an autologous unit is very difficult to replace in time for surgery.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 18; continuous question 171. Topic path: Blood bank/Standard operating procedures/Autologous donation/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: A woman begins to breathe rapidly while donating blood. Choose the correct course of action.
option_a: Continue the donation; rapid breathing is not a reason to discontinue a donation
option_b: Withdraw the needle, raise her feet, and administer ammonia
option_c: Discontinue the donation, and provide a paper bag for donor to breathe slowly into
option_d: Tell her to sit upright, and apply a cold compress to her forehead
explanation:
This woman is hyperventilating; therefore, the donation should be discontinued. A paper bag should be provided to the donor to breathe into to increase the carbon dioxide in the donor’s air.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 11; continuous question 164. Topic path: Blood bank/Select course of action/Donor processing/Donor adverse reactions/3.

subject: blood_bank
question: Which of the following is an acceptable time in which a unit of whole blood is collected?
explanation:
A unit of whole blood should be collected within 15 minutes.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 15; continuous question 168. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Collection/1.

subject: blood_bank
question: Can an autologous donor donate blood on Monday if he or she is having surgery on Friday?
option_a: Yes, he or she can donate up to 72 hours before surgery
option_b: No, he or she cannot donate within 7 days of surgery
option_c: Yes, he or she can donate, but only a half a unit
option_d: No, he or she cannot donate within 5 days of surgery
explanation:
An autologous donor can donate up to 72 hours before expected surgery.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 4 Immunohematology; section 4.8; book question 14; continuous question 167. Topic path: Blood bank/Apply knowledge of standard operating procedures/Autologous donation/2.

subject: blood_bank
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch4_immunohematology/panel_1.png]]
Refer to Panel 1. Which antibody is most likely implicated?
explanation:
The pattern clearly fits that of anti-Jkb, an antibody that usually reacts best at IAT. The weaker reactions are caused by the dosage effect found on cells that are heterozygous for the Jkb antigen.
